exercise.name: One-Arm Dumbbell Row

reference.title: Dumbbell Single Arm Bent Over Row
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Back, equipment Dumbbell, exercise type Strength

exercise.mechanics: Compound (shoulder extension, scapular retraction, elbow flexion)

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you row, inhale as you lower.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s up, 0.5 s squeeze, 2 s down

prescription.load: User-chosen dumbbell; stop about 1-3 reps short of failure (RIR 1-3)
prescription.progression: Add load or reps; add a pause at the top

cues.text: Left knee and left hand on the bench, right foot on the floor, back flat and about level, right arm hanging straight.
Breathe out and drive the elbow up and back toward the hip, close to the body.
Squeeze the shoulder blade back; the dumbbell reaches the side of the lower ribs.
Breathe in and lower under control until the arm is straight.
Let the shoulder blade glide forward a little, keep the back flat, repeat.

mistakes.mistake: Twisting the trunk open to lift the weight
mistakes.fix: Keep both shoulders level; use a lighter dumbbell.

mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back or shrugging the shoulder to the ear
mistakes.fix: Keep a flat back and pull the elbow toward the hip, not up to the ear.
Keep the elbow close to the body for the lat-focused row.

kinematics.norm: Back flat, roughly parallel to the floor, supported by the bench (clinical opinion)
From nearly straight to about 90 degrees at the top (clinical opinion)
Elbow passes the line of the back with the upper arm close to the trunk (clinical opinion)
Controlled, about 1 s up and 2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #483712, Dumbbell Single Arm Bent Over Row, video (movement reference)
Fenwick, Brown & McGill 2009, comparison of different rowing exercises: trunk muscle activation and lumbar spine motion, load and stiffness (J Strength Cond Res 23(2):350-358)
Lehman et al. 2004, variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises (Dynamic Medicine 3:4)

cautions: Stop if sharp pain, numbness, tingling or giving-way occurs.
The dumbbell load is your choice: pick a weight you can move with the form shown for every rep.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
Low-back pain: the bench support usually makes this row easier on the back than a free-standing bent-over row (Fenwick 2009 measured the highest lumbar load in the standing bent-over row).
modify: Shoulder pain: shorten the range at the top and keep the elbow close.
Wrist discomfort on the support hand: make a fist on the bench or rest on the forearm.

muscleNotes.lats_r: Main shoulder extensor: pulls the elbow from in front of the shoulder back to the side of the trunk.
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_r: Retract the shoulder blade at the top. Rows gave the highest middle trapezius/rhomboid activity of the pulls tested by Lehman 2004.
muscleNotes.post_deltoid_r: Helps extend the shoulder as the elbow passes the trunk.
muscleNotes.biceps_r: Flexes the elbow to about 90 degrees; neutral grip shares the work with brachialis and brachioradialis.
muscleNotes.core: Brace so the trunk does not twist toward the working side. A one-armed (cable) row challenged the torsional capacity of the trunk muscles with a low lumbar load (Fenwick 2009).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: Resist trunk rotation as the weight comes up on one side (Fenwick 2009).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Resist trunk rotation as the weight comes up on one side (Fenwick 2009).
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_r: Hold the flat back; the bench takes much of the load off the low back.
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_l: Hold the flat back; the bench takes much of the load off the low back.
muscleNotes.triceps_l: The support arm stays straight and pushes into the bench.
